_status: The v1 numeric floors were TESTED AGAINST PROFESSIONAL PRESETS AND REFUTED. They are removed, not tuned.
_what_happened: v1 turned the rulebook's adjectives into absolute parameter floors: amp
level at or above -6 dB, clean reverb at or above 25 percent, and so on.
Every number sat just above a value the owner had rejected in one build
(issue #50), which felt like sound provenance at the time.
Checked against 104 scenes from 13 presets of AustinBuddy's '25 pack,
read off the owner's own FM9, the floors raised 196 FAIL findings against
work that is professionally voiced and gig-ready. 104 of 104 scenes failed
the amp-level floor. The clean reverb floor of 25 percent exceeded the
_why_it_cannot_work: DISTORT_LEVEL is an output trim, not loudness. The pack pins
DISTORT_MASTER at 10.00 (median across all 104 scenes) and uses amp level
to compensate, so a harder-driven scene reads QUIETER by that parameter:
amp_level median   master median   drive median
Leads sit lowest precisely because they are driven hardest. A floor on
that parameter punishes correct gain staging.
The decisive comparison. The build the owner REJECTED versus the pack he
would GIG, on the values v1 policed:
They are indistinguishable, and the rejected build has MORE reverb and
delay. No threshold on these parameters can separate them, because the
difference lives in gain staging, amp model and voicing.
_conclusion: Issue #50 cannot be closed with parameter thresholds. 'Too quiet' is a
property of AUDIO, and nothing here measures audio. Answering it honestly
needs measured output, which is the re-amp capture path in issue #56.
_nothing_active: This file is a RECORD, not a policy. Nothing reads it for enforcement any more. The relational lead-versus-rhythm idea already existed as rule 10 in fm9/tone_review.py, so the v1 experiment contributed no surviving check. It is kept so the approach is not tried again without first beating the evidence.
